speechtext: -of a member of parliament or even any intelligent or semi-intelligent person suggesting that it is a breach of a minister's oath of office to say when council gets through with its work, on the ground that two ministers might speak differently and there would be disclosure of secrets?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Does not the right hon. leader of the opposition, as an ex-Prime Minister, know that the clerk of the Privy Council is aware when the cabinet adjourns-

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Of course.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: -rather than the ministers of the Crown who attend cabinet meetings?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
Of course the clerk
knows, and the reporters outside know, and anybody else can know who wants to. The ridiculous thing is that anybody would suggest that it is a breach of oath to tell.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: I know the hon. member never suggested that. The only suggestion I make to him is this: If he has a question to ask I will be willing to answer it. If he has nor he can make long enough speeches himself without interjecting stlill others into my remarks.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
If there is any gentleman in
this House that can make lengthy speeches without saying very much it is the right hon. leader of the opposition.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
Now, I desire to come to a review of what is before the House for a decision, a decision as far-reaching in its importance, as impressive in its nature, as any at which this House has ever been called upon to arrive. It is first necessary that we fully understand just where we are placed and what it is we have to decide. We all recall the circumstance of the 22nd of May. We recall the definite allegation advanced in constitutional form against a minister of the Crown by an hon. member of this House. I will read the summation, of the allegation and the importance of these words I desire with all deference to impress as forcibly as I can upon hon. members. They have been quoted frequently, but I am unable to make my remarks orderly without inflicting their repetition upon the House once more. The allegation is in the following words:
The Honourable James Murdock, Minister of Labour, did withdraw from the Home Bank at its Ottawa branch on the 15th day of August, 1923, two days before such bank's failure, thousands of dollars on deposit therein to his credit, using certain informa-

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
tion he had received, as such minister, of the likely immediate failure of said bank, and had received advantage and profit to himself to the extent of such withdrawals, contrary to his obligations as such minister in derogation of his office and the honour, dignity and traditions of parliament.
This was the charge made. The precise facts which the hon. gentleman set out to prove are there stated, that the money was withdrawn on this date, that this date was two days before the failure, that the result of the withdrawal was to be of advantage to the minister to the extent of thousands of dollars, and that the money was withdrawn by reason of information received by the Minister of Labour as minister of the Crown. The hon. member for West Hastings said, "These facts I am prepared to prove on my responsibility as a member. I call upon the House to give me a committee, on the assumption therein recited that those facts establish that the minister's conduct was contrary to his obligation as such minister and in derogation of his office and the honour, dignity and traditions of parliament. I submit that the House having passed the resolution took the ground that those facts if they could be established did bring home to the minister that he had acted contrary to his obligations and contrary to the honour, dignity and traditions of parliament

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: I ask the hon. member whether it is not a fact that evidence was given before that committee that the Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons (Mr. Gordon) had been in conversation with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock)?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: I do not mind hon. members opposite interrupting me, because they want to back up the leader of the opposition. I ask whether or not the Minister of Labour had information-

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Although I suppose the right hon. leader of the opposition is well able to defend himself, I would ask the hon. senior member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) to allow him to proceed.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: When the hon. member makes assertions that are not correct, surely I have a right to correct him.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
I would suggest that
some hon. members be delegated to take care of the hon. senior member for Halifax.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
The only answer I have to
make is that the country should be delegated to take care of my hon. friend-to put him where he belongs.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: We are past the time for discussion as to whether these acts constitute a violation of the obligations of the office of a minister of the Crown, We have already referred those allegations for investigation, to ascertain whether they are true or not, on the assumption that they do constitute a violation of the obligations of a minister of the Crown, and in derogation of his office and the honour, dignity and traditions of parliament. Consequently it is only wasting time to debate whether or not, providing the facts are true, an offence has been committed. The House has passed on that already. But if it were a matter of argument, is there any hon. member of this House who is going to say, or who believes, whether he will say it or not, that a minister of the Crown can use information obtained as such minister to his own advantage, whether to avoid a loss or to make a profit? I do not say that because a minister hears something in council he therefore never can use it. Nobody suggests that, but if it is something which he receives as a minister of the Crown, which he would not otherwise be entitled to receive, then he cannot use it whether for his profit or to save a loss.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: He did not.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
And the minister receiving this information, being forbidden under the act -to make use of it for the purpose and advantage of others, certainly could not make use of it for his own advantage. What I am seeking to impress upon the House is that the whole question is whether t'he information received was received as a minister, and must be treated as secret information when so received. The point made by the member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) does not come in at all. Certainly if one hears about a ship going down, that is something which he is at perfect liberty to tell his neighbour, his wife or anybody else, but information which he cannot divulge to anybody else, he cannot use for his own advantage. It is an absurd argument to be addressed to the intellects of intelligent people to say that he can use this information to save his own money, to see that he

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
does not lose anything, but cannot use it to make a profit. I do not really know how to argue a matter of that sort. It does not appeal to one's mind at all. For example, suppose I am in the stock market, and I know that a duty is going to be imposed upon certain goods made by a firm in which I have some stock. I get that information as a minister of the Crown. I am not at liberty to tell anyone else. Would anyone suggest that I am at liberty to go out and buy more stock in that concern, knowing there will be an advance in price the minute the budget is delivered? An hon. member (Mr. Arcbamlbault) shakes his head in the negative. Let me put another question. Suppose I am a large stockholder in another concern, and I find that the tariff is going to be taken off the article it manufactures. I receive the information in council, and I know that the minute the budget is delivered, down will go the stock. Am I at liberty to go out and sell my stock so as to avoid a loss?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: That is never done.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Archambault) shakes his head in the negative. Certainly I cannot. The moment he shakes his head he admits, and his intellect would compel him to admit, that both these cases are precisely in the same category-the making of a gain and the avoiding of a loss. When one is brought home it has the same effect precisely as the other. The point is that the minister cannot use for his own advantage information he receives as minister. There is no use wandering into other fields. This matter is closed, I think, so far as this point is concerned.
I ask hon. members to note that there is no crime charged, no offence against the criminal code. An offence is charged against the traditions, the honour and the dignity of parliament. The offence charge is a malfeasance in office on the part of a minister of the Crown. What another man can do a minister of the Crown cannot do. The traditions of parliament, his duty to the public, deny him that right. When he goes into a cabinet he takes upon himself an obligation never to use information received there, an obligation to which he does not swear, but one which is as binding upon his conscience as any obligation man ever took upon himself. Therefore, we know the measure of the offence charged. The consequences of guilt we all know. I do not think I need expound them, either by textual reference or precedent. I
therefore come to discuss whether or not these allegations of fact, which undoubtedly if proved, establish the guilt charged in the indictment, are brought home. I say, first of all, that they are brought home, if anything can be brought home at all, by circumstantial evidence. We find the person charged proven guilty of this offence, whatever it is, by inference from circumstances proven. The hon. member for Welland says: "Did you ever know of a man being found guilty by inference?" I say in this House as one who has had some experience in law- but if one had none at all, the ordinary reader would know this just as well-that ten men are convicted on inference for one who is convicted by the seven senses. Ten are found guilty because of circumstantial evidence out of which the inference of guilt comes for one found guilty in any other way. Let us inquire: Are the circumstances such that the reasonable man will know that guilt is established or are they not? The undisputed facts, of course, I do not need to rehearse-the fact of the deposit of the money, of its lying there from about the 3rd July until the 15th August, only trifling amounts being with-dravrn in the meantime. Its withdrawal on the 15th day of August-this is admitted. Its withdrawal in cold cash on the 15th day of August; its withdrawal and deposit immediately in a larger and stronger bank-all this is admitted. It is admitted moreover that its deposit was in the name of a secretary "in trust". There is an explanation of this given and I will discuss the explanation later. It is admitted still farther that the fact of the impending failure of the bank came to the knowledge of members of the government, not all, on the night of the 14th August, in all its horror and all its pregnancy, and that those facts were so startling that the Prime Minister, to use his own words, stood aghast. That the bank failed is, of course, admitted. That tremendous suffering and hardship have followed in its trail, everybody knows and everybody has known right back from the last days of August to this hour. The loss of those depositors, thousands of them poor working people, the sufferings and agony entailed, all have known and known, not since the 17th or 14th of May but since the bank failed in August last. It is known as well that, upon there being mooted in the press an allegation that a minister of the Crown had taken advantage of his position to save his owrn money, and the Minister of Labour being accosted by a reporter and asked if he was the man, he stated that he withdrew the money, but that he withdrew it in the

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
ordinary course for the purpose of paying on a house. I have used his language on the record. Of course nothing can be disputed which took place in this House on the 22nd day of May.
I now come to the one fact around which the discussion, so far as it is relevant or useful, revolves. Has it been established! by satisfactory evidence that the minister acted on information gained as a minister of the Crown? I do not think anything else is worthy of debate. All other talk will only confuse.	Is the evidence on this feature
satisfactory or is it not? What is the evidence? First of all there is the evidence of the directors who, on the night of the 14th, informed at least three ministers of the Crown of facts so startling that, on the admission of all three, they were facts that should be brought to the attention of their other colleagues of the government, facts so startling and important that two of them stated on their oath that, if they failed to bring them before their colleagues, they would be derelict in their duty. I will quote to prove this, if I am asked or challenged, from the evidence sworn to here by these ministers, evidence they could not help but swear to, evidence every word of which was undoubtedly true. And even if that evidence had not been given, every one of us would have known that it was a fact anyway. Is anybody so childish, so hopelessly innocent and mentally uncouth as to imagine that, it being brought to the attention of the government that a bank was to fail in the course of one, two days or hours, they would not have brought the subject before their colleagues at their first meeting? No one who has ever had anything to do with a government will ever be told that, or, at least, not face to face. The absurdity of such a suggestion affronts the intellect, affronts one's common sense. This bank collapse was the most startling event in two years :n the commercial life of Canada, and imagine, after ministers are apprised of it, they conceal it from their colleagues for any time at all! No, they frankly say: Our duty certainly was to consult them. The Prime Minister tells us the view he took of the matter and the view he expressed to the delegates who came from the bank. That was his view; but he very properly, inevitably stated, could not avoid stating that before anything final was determined upon as regards a subject of such colossal importance to the people of Canada, he was bound to lay the matter before his colleagues.
On the afternoon of the 15th August, the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was

to go to Montreal on this very matter and, associated with the Home Bank delegates, to lay the truth before the Bankers' Association. For the purpose of their discussion of the subject, for the purpose of his own information, he acquires from the directors that morning in the hotel a written statement of the position, supplementary, perhaps, or perhaps only complementary of the presentation of the night before. It was already arranged that he was to go to Montreal. That is the evidence on record. What are his instructions to be down there? Those will be determined, and I ask hon. members: Where? Would they not be determined in cabinet council? Why, for the government even to intimate to this House that the final action, the final conduct of the government in this regard, even before the meeting with the Bankers' Association in Montreal, would be determined save when all council were consulted, would be an admission of an inappreciation of public duty. No, one only needs to argue simply for the sake of putting it in print that the matter came up in council. Common sense teaches everybody that it must have come up in council before the Acting Minister of Finance could go to Montreal, especially in view of the impending almost instantaneous collapse of a financial institution in this country.
But what is the other evidence? Immediately the sitting is through, about 12.45 p.m., the minister takes his route right across to the Home Bank, signs his cheque, lays it down, demands his money, demands $4,050 in bills. I ask hon, members to remember not only the bills, but the exact amount, $4,050. The haste of the minister immediately after council is some indication in itself of what council considered while in session. There is the evidence of the minister and, perhaps, I had better read it exactly. I will read first what the minister says in respect of what he considered his duty. At page 75 the minister after reciting the fact of the withdrawal and the fact of having heard reports in February and March, and having intimated his decision to pay back the money, says this:
I think, Mr. Chairman, that covers the statement necessary. I might say, of course, that I am precluded by my oath as a cabinet minister from intimating in any way whether any questions in relation to the Home Bank of Canada were or were not discussed at either of the cabinet meetings of August 15th which I have said I attended.
Thus in his first carefully prepared statement, the only statement he made save on cross-examination, 'he emphasized in the clearest, simplest terms that he was precluded

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
by his oath of office from saying a word as to whether this matter was or was not discussed. And in the face of that every hon. member who has stood to defend him in this House has asserted that, a page or so afterwards, he violated what he considered his oath, stating that the matter had not been discussed there at all. Are those gentlemen doing justice to the minister who stand and plead in his defence, what would be a violation of what the minister himself believed to be his oath? Or are those doing the minister justice who refuse to believe that he deliberately violated that oath? The whole circumstances show that when the minister stated, as reported on, the next page, that he had not discussed the matter with others, he meant others outside the cabinet council; and they who argue otherwise attribute to him a breach of what he believed to be his oath of office.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Am I to understand that the right hon. member's contention is to the effect that the Minister of Labour under oath stated that the matter had not been discussed?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: No, I do not think that he said so. Does not the hon. member agree that the Minister of Labour never intended to say that the matter never was discussed?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
Knowing my right hon. friend so well, I would rather not give an answer just now.
Mr. MBI'GHEN: That is the safest course, perhaps. I stated very clearly what I thought the minister wished to convey. I do not think that the minister wanted to leave that impression at all; if he did then he is guilty of something which I think is worse than even what he is charged with by the hon member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter). I do not think he violated his oath, but in view of his own statement he did violate it, if those who have spoken in his defence are right in their contention. Let me quote from the evidence. The conversation with the Deputy Speaker had been under review-this conversation which referred to the Home Bank as a lame duck, the nearest approach to the specific that was brought out in evidence. Then the evidence continues:
Q. And after getting information from Mr. Gordon did you get any further information?-A. No.
Q. You say "No"?-A. No.
Q. Of any kind or description-or anywhere?-A. Not that would form my opinion in regard to the matter.
Q. It may not have formed your opinion, but did you get any other information?-A. No one else had discussed the matter with me at all.
It is manifest what the minister meant; the only one he had discussed the matter with was the Deputy Speaker. And this was only two minutes after he had declared that he was unable by reason of his oath to divulge whether this subject was or was not discussed in the cabinet council by his cabinet colleagues. It is perfectly idle to argue that the Minister of Labour went on oath one minute and swore that if he said a word as to whether or not the matter was discussed at the cabinet meeting he would be violating his oath, and that the next minute he would step right forward and violate that oath as he understood it by stating that the matter had not been discussed. The minister meant nothing of the sort. The circumstances show that he never intended to convey such an impression; and those of us at least who do not wish to believe him guilty of perjury-must dismiss that view. Up to this point there is no denial at all. The facts show however that he proceeded post-haste to the bank and got his money out. These things are a clear indication, if we had not all these other facts as to the circumstances which would compel discussion that morning, that there actually was a discussion.
There are many other circumstances just as convincing as any I have cited and I am going to review them. I wonder, has it any significance that the minister withdrew $4,050? He had more than that on deposit; he had $4,150 odd on deposit at the very moment that he withdrew the amount I have stated. Now, the minister wtihdrew the money for the purpose of saving it. He admits that; there is no argument about it. Well, was he anxious lo lose the other hundred? Was he wanting to contribute that to the widows and orphans who had their deposits in the bank? Does anyone accept that explanation? The minister wanted to leave a little money in the bank. Why? The answer is, so that it would not appear as though he had withdrawn it to 3.ive it; he wanted to have at least one feature of the case which would disarm suspicion. Another circumstance worth observing is this:	I could not help thinking that the
hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) had her mind centered on one very pertinent fact. Why did the Minister of Labour when he got his money out of the Home Bank walk right past the Royal Bank to his office and not forthwith deposit it? Is anyone present with a suggestion? Here is a case for the fertile mind.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
He would not have to walk past the Royal Bank.
3660	COMMONS
Mr. Murdock and Home Bank

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: It was just two or three doors away.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
His office is west, and the
Royal Bank east, of the Home Bank.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Well, half a block away, just a few doors. Why did he go to his own office with that money in his pocket? The hon. member has not offered any suggestion and he cannot.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
He was still afraid of
banks.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
The humour of my hon. friend never fails him. But the minister's confidence in banks was quickly restored as soon as he met his secretary in his office. On
entering his own office he instructs his secretary to take the money over and deposit it in her own name in trust. This evidence did not come from the Minister of Labour; it came out afterwards. It apparently was believed that when the minister made the statement that he had withdrawn the money after leaving the council, everyone would be satisfied and there would be no need of calling witnesses from the Royal Bank. But those witnesses were called and this evidence came out, that the money was deposited in the name of the minister's secretary in trust. Then came the minister at last with an explanation. I ask hon. members to keep in mind the fact that he said not a word about this in his own evidence in chief. The explanation given of this incident is this: The reason he put bis own money in the name of another was to enable that other to draw it out without a power of attorney. He wanted the money deposited in such a manner that the other person could draw it out. And, miind you, he could not withdraw it himself without a power of attorney. I ask the House to reflect whether that is a satisfactory explanation or not. I ask hon. members to inquire of their fellows how many in this House have their own personal and private funds in the name of a secretary, of a stenographer.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Some are too cute.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
Yes, I would think so. What I say is, and I say it in all charity, this explanation does not satisfy. This explanation is not an explanation at all. A man puts his money in his own name. If he trusts someone he may give that someone a power of attorney to cheque against his account, and he directs that attorney what to draw. But why would a man residing here put his money in the name of another person so that that person would be able to draw on his funds at her will, and he could not draw 
his own funds himself? He would have to have a power of attorney from his stenographer to draw his own money! There are other circumstances, but the significance of this cannot be and is not lost on any mind in this House. This method was adopted simply as a safeguard that the facts would not so likely get out.
But there are other circumstances too. I want hon. members to keep in mind that although the money was transferred to the Royal Bank on August 15, virtually nothing was drawn out of that account until October 1. The first time any publicity was given to the circumstance was, I think, in the month of March, 1924, some six months after the occurrence itself, some six months after the whole Dominion knew of the suffering entailed in the crash of the Home Bank. When the facts came out in the press of the money going right over to the Royal Bank, the very same bills rolling back the next morning through the clearing house into the Home Bank, those facts-those allegations rather, to be fairer, came out in Toronto-I do not think they were out the same day in Ottawa-then Mr. Murdock is interviewed by a reporter of the Ottawa Journal. The reporter did not give evidence because Mr. Murdock admitted the facts. He was asked if he was the man, and he answered " yes." His explanation, and the only one, was that he drew out the money in the ordinary course of business to pay on a house. Mr. Murdock was not then on oath. I ask hon. members of this House if they think he told the truth in that statement.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Certainly he did.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: He took the money out to pay on a house?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: On a mortgage which was not due until October 1.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Why, the hon. member says Mr. Murdock took the money out to pay on a mortgage. Mr. Murdock says on oath now that he did not, that he took it out to make it safer in another bank.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
He took it out to make it
safer and to eventually pay off a mortgage on his house. Why don't you be fair?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
Yes, he took it out that it might be safer in another bank because he needed the money to pay on a house. Would it be any different if he needed the money to pay on something else? I suppose if he did not need it to pay on a house he would have left it where it was? How absurd! The

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
whole house idea was a shield put up to cover the withdrawal. The house had nothing on earth to do with the withdrawal of his money. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) knows it. If he wanted the money later to pay on another debt would he not have withdrawn it just the same? The withdrawal of the money was to make it safe. That is what he said. The simple fact is that he did not pay it until October 1.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: When the mortgage became due.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Yes; but this is all beside the point, it does not affect the issue at all. The fact is he did not pay a dollar on the house until October 1, although he protected the money on August 15. Was it frank, was it truthful on his part to tell the public that he was withdrawing the money from the Home Bank to pay on a house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
Was it not a
fact that the Minister of Labour at the time was expecting to make a trip to the West and be absent from Ottawa about the time the payment on his house would become due, and that this was his reason for removing the money as he did and leaving it in the name of his secretary who, being in Ottawa while he was absent, would be able to make the payment when it became due?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: That is not in evidence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
That is the
minister's statement to me.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Perhaps he did. I do not like this habit of the Prime Minister of fetching in evidence second hand from somebody else. But even if all that was stated in his evidence, why could he not leave his cheque to be payable when the payment became due, or why could he not send the cheque from where he was? I wonder if the Prime Minister has his money in the name of some secretary.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
As a matter of
fact, my secretary is the only one who has had my bank book for the last two years.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
So has mine, but the
bank book is in my name.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK

I have not
seen mine for the last two years.

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext: Whose name is it in?

maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK

speechtext:
If he has money in his
account he would not have any trouble. What a paltry excuse to give to the Prime Minister, that he wanted the account in the name of his secretary so he could easily pay money on a house on October 1! Why this is only added evidence against the minister. To tell that to his chief is simply adding to the evidence of his guilt. The conduct of the minister from the beginning is just the conduct of a man who knew he had done something which he should not have done. Right from the moment that he got the money out, if he felt it was something he should have done 11 p.m. and was quite right in doing, he would not have gone to his desk first in his office, farther away, he would have gone to the Royal Bank right beside him and put the money there. There is other evidence still, although I do not attach the importance to it that some do. In his evidence he stated clearly that " other circumstances developed" that day which brought t'he contemplated withdrawal to a head. Is it conceivable that he would not have told what they were, if they did not take place in council?
But there is other evidence more important still. Here are facts which I know will sink into the minds of any one who has ever had to do with a trial of any kind. If this matter never was discussed in council on August 15, it was within the power of his colleagues to have cleared Mr. Murdock in five minutes without any violation of their oath at all. The fact of evidence not coming forth which if innocence existed is available to prove innocence, is always taken in a court of law as the very best evidence of guilt. Does anybody suggest that if the matter of the Home Bank had never been discussed at that council meeting on the morning of August 15, there was anything in the oath of any minister to prevent him saying so? Nothing could be more absurd, nothing could be more ridiculous unless it be to talk about anybody being forbidden to tell who goes to council, or when council gets out. Those things are perhaps still more grotesque. I do not care

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
what Judge MeKeown said. He did not give any ruling anyway, for the matter never came before him for consideration. He was just asked whether argument in council could be given publicity to, and he very properly said no, it could not. Then incidentally he was asked, "Could they say who was present?" and he said, "I don't think that could be given in evidence." Still if he had been doing any thinking he would not have said it. 1 do not like to refer even to what was purely an aside by the judge as ridiculous, but hon. members will on a moment's reflection agree that such an aside is ridiculous. In the British cabinet, where the oath is the same as here, there is announced every morning in the papers who was at council, and officially in books I have before me it is announced who was at council day by day; and any man, at least in our time, could stand right outside the council door and report to anybody who went into council. The oath of office does not say a word as to who went to council. The oath says you cannot give out what takes place in the deliberations of council. It has nothing in the world to do with facts as to who where there, much less as to facts as to when they went in and when they got out.
Now then, does any one suggest a minister cannot say what did not take place in council? I do not claim he is compelled to say what did not take place, but he is allowed to say it if he wants to. There is nothing in the world in the oath of office which precludes the minister from telling what did not take place in council. As a matter of fact, ministers do it all the time. They stand in this House, in all governments, and say that such and such a matter was not discussed. They even, indeed, say what was discussed, and it is no violation of the oath even then. It wias the practice in our time, and I do not doubt it is yet, to give to the Press a statement as to subjects that came up at council. This was very often the practice, and a proper practice, but you cannot go further and say what this member of council said about it, and this one, and that, or give out anything that is manifestly of a confidential nature. This is what is forbidden. Now does any one really suggest that a minister cannot say what does not take place in council? If I am asked: Did you discuss in council the South Sea bubble, am I breaking my oath if I say no? The thing is too ridiculous for assertion. So that every member of the government, if the fact was that this subject was not under review, was at absolute liberty to come before that committee and to 
declare before the committee: We never discussed the Home Bank in the forenoon at all; the subject never came up. And once he did so, he had gone very far to clear his colleague of suspicion in this matter. But not one of them did so. To their credit be it said they did not. Not one of them ventured even to intimate that the subject did not come up. What is the inference? I want to ask, could inference be any stronger, could circumstantial evidence be more complete? I venture to ask those having to do with the courts of trial in this country if they could imagine evidence which would be better or more convincing evidence of the facts stated in this allegation.
The circumstances are complete from beginning to end. The evidence, I know, convinces this House. The minister may have heard something. I am not now calling in question the honour of the Deputy Speaker, but I must say it seemed very, very strange to me that this information was delayed so long. It seemed very strange to me that Mr. Murdock did not say anything about it in March, very strange. It seemed strange that he said nothing about it in this House on the 22nd of May, but assuming it is correct, does anybody imagine that he went there on the noon of the 15th of August because of a statement about the bank being a lame duck on the 9th of August? Why, these general statements of rumour are current all the time. We have heard them about various banks. Everybody knew, anyway, that the Home Bank was one of our weaker banks. We all knew the Home Bank was not a strong bank of the nature of the larger banks, but there was nothing in what the Deputy Speaker said which disclosed any fact at all upon which any man would think of anything special in the way of danger existing at the time, and the fact that the minister never bothered about it, but let all the money stay there till the whole peril was reviewed right before his eyes on the morning of the 15th-the fact that he left it there till that time shows that he did not act at all upon anything of this casual indefinite character which he heard from the Deputy Speaker away back on the 9th.
Now, the minister's contention all through has been such as adds mightily to the web that binds him to this offence. The minister has not been frank with parliament from the beginning. The minister's duty when the facts were disclosed first, when the allegations were made, was to make a statement which was

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
true, a statement which was frank and full. It was his duty to make a statement by which he could abide; but he failed to do so. On the contrary, he made a statement which was not true at all. When the matter came up in this House, by all precedents-and the minister doubtless was warned by his colleagues; he certainly should have been-his duty then, if he was not guilty of this offence, was to enter a frank denial and make a plain statement to the House of the facts, so that those facts could be submitted side by side with these allegations to the committee; but he did not do so. He read two letters to show that he returned the money, and thereupon he sat down. Was that treating parliament correctly? Was that treating parliament the way an hon. member would whose conduct in this whole concern was without blame?
There is another circumstance to which I might refer, and this is the returning of the money itself. I ask hon. members to review that fact in all its bearings. When was the money returned? On the 14th of May, 1924, in response to a letter dated the 7th day of May of the same year. A part was returned then. To the fact that a part was returned I attach no significance at all; it is just the same to me as if he had returned all on the 14th. Now I want to know if the minister would have returned that money if his conduct in withdrawing it was in his own mind absolutely right? If he did not get any information as a member of the government, would he have returned that money? Why did he return it? He tells us he returned it because he did not want others of the Home Bank to suffer while he did not. Why was he of that mind on the 14th of May, and not of that mind on the 15th of the previous August? On the 15th of the previous August, on his own statement he drew it out so that he might save himself and others suffer more. Now, didn't he? On the 14th of May he wants us to believe he returned it so that he would suffer more and others suffer less. Is it reasonable? Why was he not of that mind on the 1st of May, the 1st of April, the 1st of March, the 1st of February, and all through the intervening six or seven months? Ah! he gets a letter on the 7th day of May from the liquidator, and he is told by the liquidator that facts are alleged to him which require him to ask that the money be returned; " Is it your will," the liquidator asks, " to return it or to fight the case before the referee?" Mr. Murdock was face to face with the legal battle if he did not return that money. He was face to face with a revelation of the facts in the courts of law before a judge, face
to face with a revelation of all the circumstances surrounding this withdrawal; and so face to face with that revelation, sure to come, Mr. Murdock returns the money. Now I ask hon. members, did he return that money because his heart was moved for the other depositors or because of that revelation which otherwise was to come? I appeal to the common sense, the cold reason and sanity of hon. members of this House. Was he affected by a different comparison on the 14th of May from any that ever affected him before? Or was he not affected by the threat of the liquidator, that if he did1 not return the money he would have to face and establish his bona fides before a court of law? Thereupon he returned the money. Therefore I say, to return it under those circumstances is still another cord which binds him to the offence embodied in this allegation.
Now this House owes justice to the hon. member for West Hastings just as much, and no more, as it owes justice to the Minister of Labour. It will not do for this House to treat these matters lightly. If the House goes on record as stating that in the face of all these circumstances a minister can so act, and be acquitted, then so much the worse for the conduct of cabinets and public men in the years to come; so much the worse for the honour and repute of parliament; so much the worse for the standing of our political institutions throughout the Empire and throughout the world. A man who enters the cabinet of this country must be governed by a standard consistent with our traditions. Such a man must be governed by a standard which appertains not to others; and when he falls from the standard he must accept the penalty. Hon. members will do themselves most justice will do this government most justice, and will do the minister himself most justice to pronounce a verdict in accordance with the facts.

speechtext:
At this stage of the debate, and especially after the very complete summing up of the case by the right hon. leader of the opposition, my remarks will be very brief for two reasons: First, because most of the facts have been brought before the House; secondly, because the plea of the right hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has shown beyond any doubt that the report of the committee should be upheld. I am quite sure that my right hon. friend is not aiming at such a result; but I think that when hon. members will have scrutinized his speech, when they will have weighed his arguments, they will come to the conclusion that the decision of the committee

Mr. Murdoch and Home Bank
on Privileges and Elections was a good one and should be upheld.
Questions of privilege are probably the most important questions that could come before us. They are generally questions where the honour of one of our fellow members is at stake. We may be divided on political grounds, we may differ in principle on public questions; but in the daily intercourse among fellow members even if we are political opponents we are all personal friends. Therefore, whenever the honour of a fellow member is at stake it is always with a sense of our responsibilty, with a very heavy feeling of our parliamentary responsibility, that we approach the question and give our views thereupon.
Not only are questions connected with parliamentary privileges questions of great moment and importance on account of the reasons I have just given, but there is this other fact to be borne in mind:	Since the
great upheaval of 1914 to 1918 the institutions which have governed the world have been menaced in so many directions and by so many means, that it is the duty of every public man in any country to try and do his very best to safeguard those institutions. Therefore, whenever a question arises here which might shake the confidence of the Canadian people in their parliament that question should be dealt with in a calm and dignified manner, and without any display of partisanship. If my hon. friend from West Hastings, (Mr. Porter) whom I have know for several years, had approached this matter in the spirit which I have indicated, if hon. members on the other side had conducted this question as it should have been conducted, and had taken. the attitude which they should have taken, they would have risen far above any party spirit. I am sorry to	say I	believe this whole
matter loses the importance that it might otherwise have had because it has been a political means adopted by the Tory party in this House to try and ruin the reputation of one of the ministers of the government. Had hon. members opposite risen in this House to uphold the privileges of parliament, if they had asked us to punish one of our fellow members whose conduct had been undignified, I would have been the first to support their contention and try and help them in the achievement of that object. But since the inauguration of this matter every word which has been uttered, every move which has been made, has shown that the object of hon. gentlemen opposite is not to safeguard the dignity of parliament but simply to murder politically one of their political opponents.

What was the reason for bringing this charge before parliament? How does it come that the hon. member for West Hastings has presented himself before you, Mr. Speaker, as the champion of parliamentary dignity? I have sat in this House for seven years, I have followed the actions of the hon. gentleman throughout the proceedings of parliament whenever 1 was present. He has been always a very pleasant, genial, agreeable fellow member, but never before have I seen him showing such zeal and ardour in protecting the dignity, honour and traditions of parliament. When did the hon. gentleman discover that his parliamentary honour was ruffled, that his dignity was slighted? When did the hon. gentleman discover that our parliamentary traditions were disregarded? The hon. gentleman discovered it wdien he thought he could bring before this parliament a matter which would hurt the reputation of the Hon. Mr. Murdock, a political opponent who had encountered the enmity of the Tory party on account of his having resigned from the Board of Commerce in 1921. It has been said that the reason why the Bourbon regime in France did not succeed after the downfall of Napoleon was that the Bourbons had not forgotten anything and had not learned anything. The Tory party in this country are the best Bourbon representatives we have. They never forget a man who has hurt the party; and the Hon. Mr. Murdock, having resigned under circumstances which were hurtful to the Tory party, is to be made the victim of their revengeful spirit.
Now, examining the proceedings of the committee I will advance first the proposition that as a matter of fact the charge laid by my hon. friend from West Hastings has not been proved. In this House we cannot proceed on suspicion. We cannot base a judgment on inferences. The leader of the opposition made an appeal to those who had experience in court rooms. I have had a certain experience in the courts, and never have I heard a lawyer of any standing at the bar in my province or in any other province asking that a prisoner be convicted on suspicion or on inferences. The evidence which has to be brought before a court- and this, Mr. Speaker is the highest tribunal in Canada-is positive evidence of facts. We have the proceedings before the committee. Every word that has been uttered by the witnesses has been printed. I challenge any member of this House, no matter on which side he sits, to show that it has been proven in any way that the Minister of Labour as a matter of fact has taken an undue ad-

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
vantage of any knowledge he might have acquired a3 a minister of the Crown. We have to restrict ourselves and limit ourselves to the pertinent evidence lawfully adduced before the committee. All the witnesses who were heard were precluded from giving evidence as to what happened in council. When the decision was given by the chairman in regard to whether the witnesses could divulge the proceedings before council, my hon. friends who -it opposite to me were unanimous in saying that it was privileged-not only privileged in a qualified way, but absolutely privileged. Therefore we have no evidence whatever in the printed proceedings of what happened in council. No man in this House, no matter where he sits, or who he is, can say that it has been proven that the Home Bank matter was mentioned in council. There is no such evidence. Can we say, as we are asked to do by the leader of the opposition, "It is true there is no evidence but we can suppose." This is no matter of supposition. We have no right to suppose. We are the judges and we must weigh the evidence.
My second proposition is that even though every allegation of my hon. friend from West Hastings had been proven, even admitting for one moment that witnesses had come before the committee and told us that the Home Bank had been discussed, even admitting that after having heard the discussion among his colleagues, the Minister of Labour had 'left the cabinet chamber and gone to the bank to withdraw his money, and even admitting the whole case presented by the hon. member for West Hastings, I say that in law the charge which he has made is absolutely non-existent. There is no offence. A most extraordinary contention was brought forward by my hon. friend from York-Sun-bury (Mr. Hanson). He contended that although no evidence had been brought forward as to , what hgd happened in council, yet taking the evidence given in relation to the conversation between the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Gordon) and the Minister of Labour, if the Minister of Labour had spoken to the Deputy Speaker in his capacity of minister of the Crown, he had taken an undue advantage of his quality as minister, and he was therefore equally guilty. Let us, Mr. Speaker, consider the first proposition which is purely supposition, and then deal with the second proposition, which is totally absurd. Recently the Right Hon. Winston Churchill wrote a book about his experiences during the war. I understand that he sold his rights for an enormous sum. In that book he divulged happenings at council during the 232
war and published certain documents. Would my hon. friend contend for one moment that Winston Churchill should be expelled from parliament, if he were a member of parliament to-day?

What on earth has that
to do with this case?

If my hon. friend does
not see it-
I do not.

Then I am sorry. I
thought his legal intendment was much brighter.

I do not think anybody
else sees it.

Let us go further. The
ex-Prime Minister of England, Lloyd George, also published articles for enormous sums. He also has obtained financial advantage by using his knowledge acquired as a minister. That is a well known fact. His articles and publications are read by millions of people. Has any man in that Imperial House of Commons had the excessive sensitiveness of the member for West Hastings and raised the question as to his moral turpitude. Let us go further, Mr. Speaker. In the Marconi affair it was proved beyond any doubt that ministers of the Crown had taken advantage of the knowledge acquired as such to speculate in stock. Did the Imperial House ever raise that question? Lloyd George was mixed up in it. Lord Reading and others were also mixed up in it. Were these gentlemen ever expelled? They surely were not, because there was no offence, such as is claimed by ' the hon. member for West Hastings.
When gentlemen become members of the cabinet I understand they take two different oaths; the first as ministers, to the effect that they will administer their departments in the best interests of the public in general, and the second as privy councillors. The member for West Hastings has a right to ask the members of this House to condemn the Minister of Labour if he proves, first that his conduct was of such a nature that his departmental administration might have suffered. The hon. member certainly will not pretend that for one moment. If the department has not suffered, has the public interest suffered? Has it been shown here that the public in general has suffered through the conduct of the Minister of Labour? Has that been proved here to the satisfaction of hon. members? Has my hon. friend from West Hastings or his fellow-members in the House produced one

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
tittle of evidence to the effect that the conduct of the Minister of Labour was against the public interest in Canada? If, therefore, the Minister of Labour has acted in such a way as not to hurt departmental affairs with which he is entrusted, and if he has behaved in such a way as not to injure the public in general, we have no right to interfere. Where would be the offence?
I come now .to my third proposition. I stated first that in fact the case was not proven. I stated secondly that in law the case does not exist, and I state thirdly that the case is not practical, and we should not bother about- it in parliament. Who can go to the Minister of Labour andi complain of what he did? The depositors? My hon. friend from West Hastings is not a depositor. My hon. friend from York-Sunbury is not a depositor. I hope my right hon. friend, for whom I have great esteem, is not a depositor either.
No, nor anywhere else.

The same here. Then
what are we arguing about? Every cent that the depositors might have lost, Mr. Murdock has sent back, from a practical viewpoint, why are we wasting our time to-day? To have the hon. member for West Hastings show us that as he is getting older, he is getting wiser and purer, may be interesting, but it is costly. Has it been proven that Mr. Murdock took an undue advantage? That money in the bank was his property. He had a right to it. It did not belong to the shareholders. It did not belong to his fellow depositors. I't belonged to him and he went and got it. Supposing the hon. member for West Hastings owned a horse, and supposing he was a member of the municipal council and at a meeting of that council he heard that a thief had gone to his stall in the stable to steal his horse. He would go to the stable and, finding the thief going away with the horse, he would grab it. He would be doing only what he was entitled to do. Let us come down to ordinary common sense.
Oh, oh.

Unfortunately, we have had very little from the other side. Leaving aside partisanship, can any man in this House, being a real man, not a politician, stand on his feet and seriously, without the risk of being laughed at, claim that he would not have done the same thing as James Murdock? I say that any man who would have done otherwise would not be fit to sit in this parliament.
I come to the most extraordinary contention of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, who [Mr. Cannon.J
says that when the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Gordon) spoke to the Hon. Mr. Murdock, it was two political authorities meeting, and, therefore neither of the two should move on account of knowledge interchanged. It was not two men, two friends, meeting; it was my good friend the Deputy Speaker meeting the Minister of Labour. Therefore, if Mr. Murdock knew from the Deputy Speaker at that time that there was something wrong with the Home Bank he should not have spoken about it, and if he did, he ought to be kicked out of this House! Supposing Mr. Speaker, that instead of talking about the Home Bank, the Deputy Speaker, after having spoken about business with Mr. Murdock, had said to him: "Look here, Murdock. I forgot, your house is on fire." Mr. Murdock would have had to stay in his seat until he had ceased to be a minister! If the Deputy Speaker, instead of talking about the Home Bank, had said: "Jim Murdock, it is pouring rain," if Mr. Murdock had gone out as a minister, he would have had to leave behind his overcoat and umbrella! Are we here in parliament going to believe such nonsense, or are we going to listen to such arguments and vote accordingly?
I come now to the most farcical feature of the whole affair. To-day we have been given a standard of political morality by people who have been begging in such matters for twenty or thirty years gone by. We are going to be told what is the honour, dignity and tradition of parliament by the Tory party! I have seen good comedies, but I do not regret not having gone to any show in Ottawa to-night. I have seen a better comedy right in this House-this Tory party, this old party which is practically crushed under scandal after scandal, the party to which belongs the Canadian Pacific scandal, the Mc-Greevy scandal, the Canadian Northern scandal, the War-time Elections scandal, the wartime scandals. Why did the hon. member for West Hastings, instead of dragging before the bar of this House the honoured name of the Minister of Labour, if he wanted to be sincere and to reform political morality in this country, not bring before the bar of this House and of public opinion his former leader, Sir Thomas White? If the hon. gentleman had exhibited the same standard of morality with the same strictness in the case of Sir Thomas White as in that of Mr. Murdock, instead of its being an honour for Mr. Murdock to resume his seat, something quite different might have happened to Sir Thomas White, and my hon. friend knows what I am referring to. The Tory party is going to tell us what political morality is!

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank

Sir Thomas White is
not a member of this House. If the hon. gentleman is making a reflection on him, he should make it at least specifically. I do not know what the hon. member is referring to, but as an associate I do not know of any more honoured name that ever adorned the public life of Canada than that of Sir Thomas White.

I know whereof I speak.
This was a Minister of Finance, amongst whose followers was the hon. member for West Hastings and who knowing the condition of the Home Bank, never moved, never did anything to save the depositors, a man who, as minister of the Crown, had the whole responsibility and who, after being a minister, became the lawyer of the same bank and received SI,500 for coming here to try to get a Liberal government to save from ruin a bank that he, as a minister, refused to interfere with, for what reason I do not know. The hon. member for West Hastings should find out from his friend himself. This is the party in front of us, the reformers, the moralists, the scrupulous people who, meeting the Hon. James Murdock, have to cross the street because they are afraid of being contaminated! The spectacle that we are being shown to-day is one at which the people of Canada will ha've a good laugh because it is a joke. It is ridiculous, not only on account of the party, but on account of the leader of that party. I was listening to my right hon. friend, for whom I have great consideration; but when my right hon. friend started talking about morality, if it had not been for the honour, dignity and traditions of this House, I might have burst out laughing. Here is a gentleman who in 1917 did things of such a nature that to translate them he used language that nobody knew in Canada. Are we going to hear from this gentleman what political morality should be?

I would advise the hon.
member to have some regard for the truth. The hon. member now is stating what he must know to be untrue. I suppose he refers to a miserable filibuster of the late hon. member for Cape Breton which failed about as ignominiously as anything ever did in this House, an allegation which not only he failed to prove but which was absolutely denied and which turned out to be based wholly on a forgery.

Is my right hon. friend
in a position to tell us what language the telegram was written in?
232*

I had nothing to do
with the telegram at all. The signature to it was not mine. There was no signature except initials, and they were not mine, they were never written with my authority, and I knew nothing about the matter. The hon. member knows that.
The right hon. gentlemen's secretary no doubt had power of attorney.

I would suggest to the
hon, member that he adhere to the issue if he has anything to say about it.

I am sure my right hon.
friend is not very well pleased to have the issue enlarged with himself included in it. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have detained the House long enough.
Go on.

Let me sum up the case
thus:	First, the facts do not bear out the
charge in law; secondly, there is no charge; in the third place, there is no practical advantage in discussing the matter; fourthly, it is ridiculous and absurd for our friends opposite to presume to teach us anything touching public morals. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say Ithat this incident is to be regretted. Our friend who sits on this side (Mr. Murdock) has been out of the House for a considerable time; and not only has he been absent from the House, but in his own home I am sure that much anxiety must have prevailed by reason of the very hard conditions under which the Tory party conducted this investigation. Let us hope that this will be the last instance of excessive partisanship.
Oh, oh.
I hope the hon. gentleman will take this matter seriously; it will do him a whole lot of good.
I am still thinking of you.

Let us hope that should
political warfare continue it will at least stop at the door of private life and before the sanctuary of family ties.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This whole matter has
been so ably and fully reviewed that it would be short-sighted, indeed, to attempt in any way to go over the ground which already has been so fully and comprehensively traversed. However, I should not like the debate to con-

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
elude without saying a word or two as to the significance of the decision we are being asked to make. As has been mentioned, it is not only the character and the good name of an hon. member of this House that are at stake in the report which the committee on Privileges and Elections have brought in and which we are being asked to pass upon; there are also involved the honour, the dignity and the traditions of this parliament. We are called upon to consider very carefully principles of which account should be taken in judging this matter. I shall not attempt to give views of my own as to the principles that should govern the House in coming to its decision, but I shall refer to one or two authorities whose names are greatly respected and whose opinion should be respected in reference to the judging of matters of privilege and personal reputation of members of parliament.
In 1891 a charge was brought against an hon. member of this House who was a minister of the Crown. The charge, which was a very serious one, was to the effect, not, that while he was in office as a minister, but that previously as a private member of the House, he had had an interest in a government contract and had profited materially from the fruits of that contract. That was the charge that was brought against him and which the government of the day was being asked to investigate. In answer to the request for an investigation, no less a parliamentarian thaD Sir John Thompson, who a little later led the party which my right hon. friend opposite (Mr. Meighen) leads at the present moment, gave his views to the House as to the principles which should govern in determining a matter of this kind. I shall read one pertinent paragraph, I think hon. members will recognize in a moment wherein it bears upon the question we are considering. Sir John Thompson said, as reported in Hansard of September 23, 1891, volume 3, page 5946:
I am willing to treat this motion coming now, as if it were a motion placed on the order paper and reached in due course, and I shall ask the judgment of the House upon it with regard, not to any technical rule of order, but to the decision that the House should come to as the judge of its own privilege, and the judge of its own jurisdiction; feeling sure that the House will be careful to keep in mind the cardinal principle laid down from the time that the privileges of members and the privileges represented by members came to be appreciated-the cardinal principle that the House has power, where members have been guilty of a positive crime, or have offended against the laws and regulations of the House, or have been guilty of fraudulent or other disgraceful acts which proved that they were unfit to exercise the trust which their constituents had reposed in them, and unfit to continue to associate with the other members of the legislature;-to exercise its control: but remembering, too, the cardinal

principle which runs side by side with it and is of equal va-lue for the preservation of the liberty of constituencies and of members, that it is not for the House in the exercise of that jurisdiction to create a new disability or to enquire into the private transactions of members of the House.
That was the view Sir John Thompson took of how parliament should consider its rights and its duties in discussing matters affecting its honour and traditions; he held that it was not for parliament to create a new disability or to inquire into the private transactions of members of this House. I ask hon. members whether, the particular act to which the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) has referred, falls into any category other than that of a matter in the nature of a private transaction, an action which, as the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) has just pointed out, was one that concerned wholly and exclusively the minister's own property. The minister was dealing as an individual with property that was exclusively his own in a transaction which was entirely a personal and private one. It was not a public transaction or concerned with any public matter, it was altogether personal and private with respect to property which belonged exclusively to the hon. member concerned. Now, that is true wholly irrespective of where the hon. member got the information, how he got it or any question of the kind. Are we at this time in interpreting the principle of upholding the honour and traditions of parliament, to declare that in so doing it is part of the duty of parliament to inquire into the private transactions of a member of the House with respect to a matter which relates itself en-*triely to his own private business?

I think my hon. friend will admit that when the hon. member for South Lanark sits here under the writ which called on the people of South Lanark to return their representative, it does not lie with this parliament to turn out that representative and disfranchise that constituency except under the law, under the constitution, or under precedent which any man can cite.

A minister of the Crown makes a good many sacrifices in the public interest that he may give his entire time and attention to public affairs. But I submit that it is going very far to suggest that a minister of the Crown must not, in that capacity, exercise the same prudence with respect to his own property and his own family as he would be expected to exercise as a private individual.
Now I ask hon. members if they disagree with that view. If they do not disagree with it, how can they, regardless altogether of where the Minister of Labour may have obtained the information which led him to act with respect to his own property as he did,'-how can they, I say, assert that he has violated some obligation as a minister of the Crown and thereby has violated the honour, the dignity and the traditions of this House? That, it seems to me. is a broad principle we are called upon to consider, and I submit that members should in this matter exercise just the same reasonableness and fairness in forming their judgment as they would in regard to any other matter which may come before them for consideration.
Speaking of these matters of honour and dignity and tradition, there is a motto with which, I think, we are all more or less familiar; it is a motto which finds its place on the royal coat of arms, it is a motto which we have learned to respect from our earliest days-honi soit qui mal y pense; let evil be to him who evil thinks. We can start out with the assumption that the hon. Minister of Labour is a dishonest man, that he has criminal instincts, that his purpose in public life is to enrich himself; or we can start out with the belief-which those of us who know him best hold in strongest measure-that he is among the most scrupulously honest of men and the most fearless and chivalrous. What has been the record of the Minister of Labour? He started life with very little in the way of personal means, with very little assistance at his command, but by his industry, his integrity, and his honesty he won the confidence of his fellow working men, not in tens or in hundreds but in thousands over the whole of this continent. He was entrusted with part control of the trust funds of the great organization of railway trainmen of which he was one of the honoured officers and leaders. When, some few years ago, he entered the service of this country as a member of the Board of Commerce he drew a salary from the government which meant a great deal to a man of his limited means. Coming down to facts the Minister of Labour is accused of having taken advantage of his position for private gain which involved loss to others. What are the circumstances? He had drawn his indemnity, and he is not overwhelmed with the goods of this earth. In that position he is like myself. He had deposited this money in the Home Bank, but he learned from a colleague in the House, Mr. Gordon, that the institution was on the eve of failure and he withdrew the money. I shall not go to hon. gentlemen opposite for a standard of honesty but I freely say that I would have done it. I am not ashamed' to say that I would have done it, and any man with a heart in his body would have done the same. The Minister of Labour is a man with a family, he has children to protect, and in drawing this money he was defrauding nobody. The bank was only the custodian of money which belonged to James Murdock who saw fit to take this money out; he owed it to his family to do so. I ask what is wrong with that proceeding?
