That the second report of the select standing committee on Privileges and Elections be not concurred in, but be referred back to the said committee with instructions tihat they have power to reconsider the same and to strike out the words "not only" and "but entirely disproved" in the last line of the third paragraph thereof.
I wish very briefly to explain the difference this would make in: the main motion, and to take a very few minutes to give my reasons for moving it. I can assure the House that at this hour I shall not impose upon them, but I feel it is necessary for me to make my position clear on the issue before us. The difference that would be made by the amendment, if adopted, would be this: That the charge submitted to the committee on Privileges and Elections for investigation, so far as it affects the honour of Mr. Murdock, would be simply found "not proved." The amendment would delete the words "not only" and "but entirely disproved."
It may be, Mr. Speaker, that my lack of
experience in parliamentary life is responsible for the fact that I have taken this charge and this discussion very seriously.

Is not what the hon.
member is endeavouring to do is to bring into this country the old Scottish verdict of "not proven?" That is about all that he is getting at,

If the hon. member will
just contain himself, if possible, I shall endeavour to explain exactly what I am getting at. When interrupted I was pointing out that I am taking this charge seriously, both in the interests of the hon. member against whom the charge has been made, and in the interests also of the honour and dignity of parliament, which it is alleged has somehow been impaired. I say I feel as a member of this House a great responsibility first when I think that perhaps by some vote of mine the honour and dignity of parliament may be impaired; and in the second place, I feel a great responsibility when I think that a vote of mine may possibly inflict an irreparable injustice upon an hon. member.
I have listened to the arguments of the prosecuting attorney, so to speak, and also to the arguments of those who have defended the hon. gentleman who has been charged. I have tried to have regard to the legal aspects involved in the honour and dignity of parliament. and I have been trying also to pay due attention to the human phase of the situation, and I have come to a certain conclusion. That conclusion may not be, strictly speaking, a legal conclusion, but I hope 'it will be regarded as possessing reasonable common sense, and that it will be as human as the situation will permit. The evidence required either to prove or disprove the charge that is made against the hon. Minister of Labour by the hon., member for West Hastings has been properly or improperly withheld. The evidence that would have made dear the situation to the House would hinge upon this question: Did the Minister of Labour use information received at a cabinet meeting in such a way as to lead to his own financial betterment and to the disadvantage of others? That is the question that in my mind leads us to the very crux of the charge. This question has not been answered. The only source from which the evidence implied in that question could have been received was from the cabinet itself, and it has been ruled that the members of the cabinet could not be questioned. That ruling, so far as I have heard has not been challenged. I am not claiming sufficient legal knowledge to say whether the members of the cabinet were improperly or properly not called, but I have to say this: Without the evidence which they might have given, if they had been called, it is impossible to decide either the honesty or the guilt of the Minister of Labour. That being so, in the absence of the only possible evidence that could enable us to come to an intelligent deci-

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
sion, the door has been left wide open for all kinds of suspicion. I feel that if I were to follow suspicion I would undoubtedly have voted for the amendment that was moved by the opposition, but not being inclined to follow suspicion what is there left for one to do? If I take the action itself it would seem to lend itself to the conclusion that there was indiscretion, weakness, or perhaps worse, on the part of the Minister of Labour. Certainly it would exhibit a type of action that is far below that which we hope from honourable and responsible public servants in Canada. If the drift of the suspicion be unfair to the minister then he must be content to suffer the disabilities that follow the iprivileges of secrecy, and the onus must be placed upon the cabinet itself to remove that suspicion from him. The secrecy which has been maintained and sustained with regard to the cabinet council may be advisable in some instances to a reasonable degree, but I maintain that such secrecy should not hold when the character of a member of the cabinet is at stake. The point is that there is not enough evidence to ensure an intelligent decision, and in the absence of evidence we are called upon to make a guess. But it will be argued, I suppose from a legal point of view, that if this is the opinion that I hold why not exculpate the hon. gentleman and vote for his exoneration? It may be contended that it is a practice, a well established axiom in law in this country that a man must be held to be innocent until he 'is proved guilty. I understand that is a generally accepted and wholly admirable rule in criminal cases. But I do want to suggest that I would be very willing to apply that same rule to this case if all the evidence that might have been given had been permitted. However, in this case I do not accept the parliamentary practice of old as a final thing, that when the character of an honourable gentleman is at stake, the cabinet could not reveal the secrets they were talking about in order to give him his liberty, or rather to clear him of the suspicion cast upon his character. I think that the evidence which the cabinet could have given had it not been considered contrary to parliamentary practice to permit their evidence would have been indispensable- in arriving at a verdict and in the absence of that evidence I find myself unable to simply say the Minister of Labour must be absolutely exonerated since we cannot have sufficient evidence to prove him guilty. Now, the other side may say "But you are bound tlo find him guilty since he cannot be exonerated." To that I also reply briefly, that I cannot justify myself in drawing an inference from evidence that was not submitted. There is the situation as briefly [DOT]as I can put it before hon. gentlemen. What about the fact then, someone will ask? Is it not so that the money was taken out? I know that this is made light of by the Prime Minister himself. It was also held as a very trivial matter by the hon. member who preceded the Prime Minister in debate. I cannot look upon the charge as being so trivial a 'thing as the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) endeavoured to make out. Even though I beg the question to the extent of saying that there is no imputed guilt to a minister who may use information which he receives in the cabinet council for his own advantage, still I am bound to say that the action of the minister in question was indiscreet and perhaps worse than indiscreet. It 'has been argued that he only took his own money. That is not true strictly speaking. The fact is that he put $4,000, or a little over, into this bank. Really he had only the right to withdraw one thousand of that since the bank could only pay 25 cents on the dollar. Only one thousand of that under the circumstances was his money. Here you may advance the human argument and say "Would not all of us have done the same thing?" I for one would not hiave done the same thing.
Some hon. MEMBERS'. Oh, oh.

Wait until I explain what
I mean by that. I am willing to admit that I, like the minister in question, would have taken the action that in my opinion looked to be best for myself. I believe that is what he did. I believe every hon. gentleman in this House in a similar position would have done the same thing. It has transpired, that the minister was very short-sighted, he took the course that was really the wor^t for himself. That is one reason why I hesitate to vote complete censure upon him; because if he had been politically wise he would not have taken that course. Whatever else he may be his action certainly proves the hon. Minister of Labour is not a good politician because if he had been a good politician he would have seen at a glance that in taking out his money he was placing himself in the position in which he now finds himself. Yes there is a human side to this question, and I want to give consideration to that very briefly. I know that the hon. member for West Hastings, who moved the amendment, did say that Mr. Murdock had forfeited all right to the sympathy either of the public or of this House. In regard to that I want to say that a man has got to go a long way before he forfeits his right to human sympathy.

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
I certainly do not agree with the view that, even if the charge had been proven to the hilt, the minister has placed himself beyond the pale of sympathy of hon. members of this House.
In closing I say that we are called upon in the lack of evidence to take a chance on the one hand of doing an injury to the honour and dignity of parliament of which we are all professedly so very jealous. On the other hand, we are called upon in the lack of evidence to take a chance of doing irreparable injury to one of our fellows. I therefore have moved an amendment which neither exonerates nor condemns. It takes the position of the old Scotch practice which permits a finding that the case is not proven. There is no other logical conclusion to which I can come. If it is argued or suggested that this position leaves a cloud of suspicion on the head of the minister, then I reply that the course is open for the minister if he be innocent and the cabinet concerned to take such action as will immediately dispel that cloud, and that action will be to give the evidence that is necessary to enable this House to come to an intelligent conclusion. That is briefly the reason for this amendment.	*

The amendment moved

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The amendment proposed by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) clearly does not go as far as the committee has stated in their opinion we should go in this House, and so far as the government, and1 I imagine all members on this side of the House who wish to support the report of the committee are concerned, we will not be able to support the amendment of my hon. friend.

I desire to
say a few words in support of the amendment before the House. As I conceive it, the question before us resolves itself into two or three propositions. In the first place, we have to 
ask ourselves what the charge is, and in the second place, has it been proved; and in the third place if proved, what can we attach to it? I am not going to trouble the House with any definition as to what the charge is. I would much rather endeavour to see what its quality is and what its definition is. To my mind it is purely a partisan charge, and that puts the impartial onlooker in a difficult position. As far as I can see, it was introduced purely in a spirit of partisanship, and as far as I have been able to see, on the other hand, it) has been defended purely in a spirit of partisanship, and that makes it very difficult for the impartial onlooker to make up his mind with regard to it.
I think that it is not the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) that is being tested at the present time. It is this system of running the business of this House, known as the two party system, whereby for nine or ten hours we have these partisan charges bandied to and fro across ithe House, while the business of the House at the end of the session is being neglected. That is the thing that is being tested before the country to-night.
There is a real human element in this discussion to-night, and that is the position of the Home Bank depositors. We have the spectacle of the two great parties in this country standing on a point of honour, and I believe the human element has been forgotten altogether. I was in (the committee this morning when the Home Bank depositors appeared before us presenting their case. We begrudgingly, perhaps of necessity, gave them two or three hours to state their case. We had to hurry them up, in order that they might place their sad story before us. Since that time we have spent nine hours in discussing a question of honour and of dignity, and in discussing it we have shot the dignity of this House all to pieces.
Now has this charge been proven? Of course, it has not been proven. Has it been disproven? Of course it has not been disproven. We have been denied access to the very place where the evidence resided. How can we form an intelligent opinion on this question when we are not allowed to enter secrets of the cabinet where the evidence rests. I think that the government made a very serious mistake in not taking this House straightforwardly into their confidence. Taking the defenders of the Minister of Labour at their own estimate, they say this thing after all does not amount to anything. If it does not amount to anything, why not make an open breast of it? I do not think the country at large will understand the defenders of the Minister of

Mr. Murdock and Home Bank
Labour standing upon precedent. Who is Judge McKeown? He may be a dignified judge of great ability, but I do not think invoking Judge McKeown or any other precedent in order to shut out inquiry will commend itself to the people of this country. I think this House has a right to know what went on inside the cabinet that night.
It is not a question of Judge McKeown's ruling or the chairman's ruling. The ministers could not give that information without violating their oath. Would the member advise us to do that?
I do not see the point of my hon. friend's remarks.
The members of the cabinet are sworn to secrecy as to what takes place in council.
Notwithstanding its importance or unimportance.

It makes no difference;
that is their oath. Does my hon. friend advise that the members of the cabinet should have violated their solemn oath?

If that is so, and if the cabinet is bound by an oath of that kind, I must withdraw my remarks, and I do so straightforwardly. I was speaking in my ignorance of the situation. But it is a very peculiar situation that forbids the cabinet to disclose its proceedings in a case of this kind.

Did not my hon. friend take
cognizance in the committee of the fact that the oath of office was read and was printed as part of the evidence?

There is nothing in the
oath to prevent a negative answer being given, as was pointed out this afternoon and not contradicted.

I suppose that oath of secrecy
is imposed in order to safeguard the interests of the nation, and I think the interests of the nation are involved in this very question. It seems to me a very far-fetched interpretation of the intention of that oath to deny the cabinet the opportunity of doing something which I think the public would have been glad to have justified them in doing. However I will leave that. I made an error in making that statement, and will pass on to other questions. If this charge were proven, what weight would be attached to it? Shall we look at this thing through the thick end of the telescope with our friends here, or through the thin end of the telescope with our friends
over there? Here is a tendency to magnify the thing out of all proportion, and over there there is a tendency to belittle it. I think that on a question of this kind it is beside the point to inquire what any one of us would do under the circumstances. I will agree that none of us is so virtuous that he could stand up here,-unless it is my hon. friend from East Calgary, (Mr. Irvme)-and say just what he would have done or would not have done under the circumstances. I think perhaps. I have done worse things in my past life than the Minister of Labour did on that occasion. But I have no desire to repeat those things. I do not admire them, and while what Mr Murdock did is apparently satisfactory to some hon. gentlemen over there, if he had felt self-possessed enough not to have done it.
I think I interpret the minds of hon. gentlemen correctly when I say that it would have been more satisfactory to them if he had not done it. There may be some kind of red-blooded virtue which says: Now that is just the kind of thing I would have done; I would have followed the human nature that is in me and have done that thing. But that is not the kind of talk that commends itself to the people of this country, because the people of this country-and we are proud of the fact- demand a high standard in our public men, and I hope that standard in our public men may remain, no matter what degree of virtue exists in us. We are not here as individuals. We are here to uphold a standard of public virtue. I am not disposed to overestimate this thing that Mr. Murdock has done. As I said, perhaps any one of us would have done it; very likely we would, but I think there is a medium course. We must look at this thing as it is. We must not underestimate it as I am sorry to have seen some of my hon. friends here to-night, nor overestimate it as some of my hon. friends to my right have done, and, I am afraid, with something of ia partisan motive. Do not let us twist it .out of its proper shape. I am not here to judge Mr. Murdock at all, but I think, perhaps, he made a mistake. I do not think the heinousness of it was so great as our friends to my right tried to make out. I think it is something that we as a House could have left to his constituents to juidge upon if they thought fit. But to make this thing an issue on .the floor of this House; to Say that the dignity of the House is involved in it, and then to throw the dignity of the House aside and to make it a moment for partisan fray, I think is what every mind here to-night that is in

possession of itself must decide against, and this is tihe only opportunity that I cm see for such minds to decide. Personally, I am going to yote for the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I thought that this was a Progressive day in parliament; that the two old parties would tear, rend and devour each other; that we would be left alone in our glory, and that it would be really a pleasant occasion. But it seems now that there is a Progressive angle to this complication. We have heard the discussion of the testimony as to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). After listening to it for a day, we have decided that he is not guilty. That is, we have decided by a very large majority of this parliament that he stands before us to-day innocent of the charge that has been laid against him.
There is this angle to the testimony that was introduced before this committee. Mr. Murdock testified that on the 9th day of August that he got certain information from the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Gordon). The Deputy Speaker testified that he gave him certain information. Mr. Murdock testified that at the time he drew out this money he had no further information on the subject. It is now proposed to say that the charge was not disproved. If the charge is not disproved, Mr. Murdock is a perjurer; he has sworn falsely to that point. Are we, who, a few minutes ago, voted that he was innocent; that he was an honest man, to vote now that his testimony as to that point was false? I do not think such a course is consistent, and I believe this amendment that the charge is not disproven should be voted down. If Mr. Murdock is an innocent man-and we have so voted-then his testimony upon that point is entitled to credit and we should give him a clean bill of health. For that reason I shall vote against the amendment.
